questions.q: You're long a stock and want to check yourself for confirmation bias. What's the best test?
choices: Read the best case against the trade
Read more posts from other holders
Re-read your own notes on the thesis
Ask a friend who is long it too
questions.answer: Read the best case against the trade
questions.why: Read the best case against the trade. Confirmation bias feeds on agreement, so the only real test is the other side. Find the sharpest bear on the name and read him all the way through. If you can answer his points with data, the chart and your levels, good. If you can't, you're likely less sure than you feel, and that's worth knowing before you add.
questions.lesson_line: Read the best case against your trade. If you can't answer it, you're not ready.

wrong.Read more posts from other holders: Other holders agree with you, so this feeds the bias. It's more of the same view.
wrong.Re-read your own notes on the thesis: Your own notes only repeat your view. The test needs a view that argues against it.
wrong.Ask a friend who is long it too: A friend who owns it will likely agree. That's more of the same view, not a test.

questions.simple: Read the best case against your trade, because only a view that disagrees can show if bias is blinding you.

reasons: Schwab and Investopedia agree; replaces a fill-in on the same idea

deeper.example: Schwab's fix is to seek out reputable views that contradict your own. If you can't make a data-backed rebuttal to the opposing view, you're likely being blinded by bias. Investopedia says the same: seek ideas that challenge your point of view.

questions.q: You bought at $50. It's $42 now, under your stop, and you swear you won't sell below $50. What decides the exit?
choices: The stop you set before the trade
How far it has fallen from your cost
What other holders of it are doing
questions.answer: The stop you set before the trade
questions.why: The stop you set before the trade. Your $50 cost is the anchor. It feels like the line that matters, but the stock has no idea what you paid. At $42 it's already under your stop, so the decision got made the day you set it. Lots of people won't sell below what they paid, even when selling is the smart move. That's loss aversion and the anchor working together. Take the stop, then judge the stock fresh, as it is now.
questions.lesson_line: Your entry price means nothing to the stock. Judge it as it is now.

wrong.The $50 you paid for it: That's the anchor. The stock doesn't know what you paid, so your cost says nothing about where it goes next.
wrong.How far it has fallen from your cost: That still measures the stock against your $50 cost. Your entry is the anchor, so it can't tell you when to exit.
wrong.What other holders of it are doing: That's herding, copying others. Your exit comes from your own stop, set before the trade.

questions.simple: Your stop decides, because the $50 you paid has become an anchor and the stock doesn't know it.

reasons: OSC anchoring page; replaces a fill-in on the same idea

conflicts: Loss aversion size: Schwab and the OSC say a loss feels about twice (OSC: twice) as strong as an equal gain; Investopedia says some studies suggest about twice but others question whether loss aversion exists or matters in practice (f77). No question keys a multiple; every key says only that losses weigh more than equal gains, which the SEC report, Nobel summary, Fidelity and Investopedia all state.

Self-attribution bias: Schwab defines it as crediting wins to skill and losses to outside forces (f44), and Gervais and Odean describe a trader taking too much credit for successes (f120); Investopedia's behavioral finance page defines self-attribution as choices based on overconfidence in one's own skill. The SEC report pairs the two ('overconfidence (self-attribution bias)'). Questions use the Schwab definition, which the paper supports.

Recency vs availability: Investopedia treats them as one bias ('also known as recency bias or availability bias', f79); Schwab and the OSC describe availability as its own shortcut. q37-q39 key recency bias and q40 keys availability bias; no question lists both as choices.

Tilt: poker players use the word loosely. Tendler (f108, f110) restricts it to anger and says 'winner's tilt' is overconfidence or fear; the poker study (f113) says negative emotions. Questions follow that narrow meaning.

The same behavior has several names: holding a loser below the stop is described as loss aversion (Schwab f42), the disposition effect (SEC f01), the original price acting as an anchor (OSC f153, which names loss aversion and the anchor together; Investopedia f83 files judging by the entry price under disposition bias) and the break-even effect (Thaler and Johnson f117). Each question's choices include only one of these, so only one key fits.

Not used: the SEC's Library of Congress report quotes Mohacsy and Lefer calling momentum investing a manifestation of magical thinking and herd behavior. That is one cited opinion about a widely studied strategy, so no question says trend or momentum trading is herding; q47 teaches herding as copying others instead of doing your own work.

Gambler's fallacy: the formal definition (f131, f148) is about independent random events. Trade outcomes are not perfectly independent, so q53 keys only the reasoning 'a win is due after a losing run', which no source supports, and never claims trade outcomes are random.
